text: Spaced review is widely recommended, but earlier comparisons often gave the spaced group more total study time than the massed group.
asserts: earlier spaced-vs-massed comparisons often confounded spacing with more total study time

text: We therefore ask whether spacing improves recall one week later when total study time is equal.
asserts: research question: does spacing improve one-week recall at equal total study time

text: In other words, the main goal of this study is to compare spaced and massed review at equal study time.
asserts: aim: compare spaced and massed review at equal study time

text: We expected spaced review to produce higher recall than massed review
because each spaced review requires retrieval after a delay.
asserts: each spaced review requires retrieval after a delay

text: The rest of this article describes the method, reports the results, and closes with a discussion.
Twenty-four adult volunteers reviewed forty word pairs, either three times in one session or once on each of three days.
asserts: massed: 3 reviews in 1 session; spaced: 1 review on each of 3 days

text: One week later, mean recall was 0.62 after spaced review and 0.41 after massed review.
These results support the prediction that spacing improves delayed recall.
However, longer total study time could also produce such an advantage, an alternative we now examine.
asserts: alternative explanation to examine: longer total study time

text: As noted in the Introduction, earlier comparisons confounded spacing with total study time, but here both groups studied for the same total time, so study time cannot explain the advantage.
asserts: total study time was equal across conditions
study time does not explain the recall advantage

text: In addition, future studies could test whether the advantage lasts beyond one week.
asserts: future work: retention intervals longer than one week
